ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Priorities in the power sector 
*41. DR. T. SUBBARAMI RE DDY:† 
SHRIMATI JAMANADEVI BARUPAL: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Ministry of Power has listed five priorities 
in the power sector during 2004-05; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, 
(c) whether rural electrification is one of the priorities of the 
Government; and 
(d) if so, what are the steps being considered to be taken in this 
regard during 2004-05? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. T. Subbarami Reddy. 
 

RAJYA SABHA [7 July, 2004] 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Rural electrific ation is the top priority of the 
Government. The other priorities include: 
• Addition to generating capacity. 
• Augmentation of National Transmission Network and creation of 
a robust National Grid. 
• Power Sector Reform with emphasis on Distribution Reforms. 
• Formulation of important policies such as National Electricity 
Policy, Electricity Tariff Policy, Rural Electrification Policy for 
speedy implementation of Electricity Act, 2003. 
• Energy Conservation measures aimed at efficient use of electricity. 
 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The Government has worked out a strategy for rural electrification 
which envisages: 
(i) Creation of Rural Electricit y Distribution Backbone (REDB), to 
ensure at least one 33/11 KV sub-station in each block 
appropriately networked and linked to the State transmission 
system; 
(ii)  Village electrification consisting of 11 KV feeders emanating from 
the 33/11 kV sub-station and at least one distribution transformer 
in every village. 
(iii)   Household electrification from the distribution transformer. 
(iv) Deployment of other technology options such as decentralized 
distributed generation for villages and remote areas where 
conventional grid connectivity is either not feasible or not cost 
effective. 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Sir, I am very happy that the hon. 
Minister has given top priority for electrification of villages in the country. 
He has also mentioned that the Government of India is determined to 
electrify all the villages in the country by 2007 and by 2009, the Government 
wanted to electrify all the 7.8 crores of households in the country. For this 
purpose, the Ministry requires Rs. 17,000 crores to meet the infrastructure

SHRI P.M. SAYEED: Mr. Chairman, Sir, we have travelled a long- 
way from 1947 when we had only 1,500 villages electrified in the country. 
Our per capita consumption was 15 kw per year. Now; we have reached 
a stage that we have been able to electrify 4,76,000 villages and our per 
capita consumption, in the year 2004, is 582 kw per year. On the 
generation side, I would like to say that we have a Very massive plan of 
capacity addition and also we have a big plan on the transmission side. 
But, on the distribution side, we are finding some difficulty. So, in order 
to remove bottlenecks, the Government of India has planned in a very big 
way to augment transmission system by linking it to the villages. The top 
priority of the Government is to reach the last village of the country. Our 
top priority is village electrification. We are paying our attention on it. For 
this purpose, we have envisaged certain strategy which helps in reaching 
to the village level. Sir, now, 44 per cent of our village households are, 
electrified. But, still, we have to cover 56 per cent of villages. Though we 
have achieved some progress in certain States, the position in five States 
is dismal. The position of un-electrified households in certain States is 
very alarming. There are five such States. I can mention the names of 
these States. The States are: Assam is having 83.46 per cent of villages 
to be electrified; Bihar is having 94.87 per cent...

THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (DR. RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Ministry of Rural Development is presently implementing the 
following major schemes for poverty alleviation, employment generation, 
area development and infrastructure development in the rural areas of the 
country so as to bring about holistic development and overall improvement 
in the quality of life of rural poor:— 
• Swarnajayanti Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY); 
• Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY); 
• Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY); 
• Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY); 
• Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP); 
• Watershed Development Programmes (IWDP, DPAP & DDP); 
and 
• Central Rural Sanitation Programme (CRSP). 
(b) The SGSY is the major on-going programme for the self- 
employment of the rural poor. The objective of the programme is to bring 
assisted Swarozgaris above the poverty line by mobilizing them into Self- 
Help Groups, training, skill development and provision of income generating 
assets through bank credit and Government subsidy. Marketing of products 
made by SGSY beneficiaries has been one of the major concerns under 
the programme. As such the Minist ry of Rural Development has been 
organizing SARAS Fairs at the national and regional levels and Gramshree 
Melas through CAPART District Rural Development Agencies (DRDAs) 
are authorized to utilize Rs. 5 lakhs annually for professional inputs related 
to marketing research, value addition, product diversification etc. In addition 
DRDAs can utilize the infrastructure funds for organizing local fairs for 
sale and exhibition of products made by Self-Help Groups/Swarozgaris. 
The Ministry has also developed market ing infrastructure for providing 
opportunity to the beneficiaries to sell their products. 
8 

[7 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) These fairs have provided rural artisans a platform to sell their 
products beyond the limits of the local markets and also helped them in 
getting exposure to the market and marketing techniques. It has introduced 
them to new designs and better methods of packaging. The rural artisans 
also learn from each other through sharing of experience.

Snags in Jaguar Engine 
*43. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether complaints of snag in the engine of Jaguar aircraft 
have been reported; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken to remove the defects immediately? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Like any other aircraft system, routine snags have been reported on 
the engine of Jaguar aircraft also. Rectification of these snags is carried 
out at the unit level on a day to day basis. 
The only major problem faced by some of the Adour Engines installed 
on Jaguar aircraft pertains to low thrust. This problem has been reported 
on about 10% of these engines. 
A Study was ordered in September, 2002 to find out the reasons for 
12 

[7 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
such low thrust and to suggest remedial measures. The study team 
comprising representatives of Indian Air Force, Hindustan Aeronautics 
Limited, Directorate General of Aeronautical Quality Assurance and M/s 
Rolls-Royce have suggested a number of remedial measures. All these 
measures have since been implemented. As a result, the problem of low 
thrust has been reduced considerably. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR RE DDY: Sir, I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister whether all the Jaguars have been examined 
by the experts? If so, what were the defects noticed leading to several 
crashes? 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, it is a normal practice that 
whenever certain snags are developed, there is arrangement of rectifying 
those snags in the aircraft and it is almost part of the avionics. If there are 
minor snags, those are rectified in the base unit itself. And, if there are 
major snags, those are rectified in the organisations under the HAL. so 
far the snags in the areas of fuels are concerned, those are rectified in 
the units at Lucknow, and with res pect to the avionics, those are 
rectified in the unit of HAL at Bangalore. The major problem that jaguars 
had at initial stage, for which these complaints came that the power which 
was generated by the engine was low, that is why, it was called 'low-
power, low-thrust'. And, after that, a Study Team was appointed with the 
experts consisting of the representatives of HAL, Rolls-Royce, Air 
Force and other organisations. They made recommendations and 
after those recommendations being fully implemented, the snags have 
come down and reduced substantially. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR RE DDY: Sir, I want to know 
whether improper command and control was responsible for the mid-air 
collusion of two Jaguar fighters on April 2nd. If so, the steps taken to 
prevent such crashes in future? 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, it is unfortunate that on 2nd April, 
two Jaguars crashed and as per the language of the Indian Air Force, the 
accident was 'category one', that means, it is beyond repair. What happened, 
in the formation of four, these two Jaguars collided with each other as a 
result of which they met with this crash and it is unfortunate that both the 
pilots were injured. I hope they will recover. The Court of Inquiry is in 
progress and till I get the Report of Court of Inquiry, it is difficult for me to 
indicate what were the reasons and whether there was any human failure 
or there was a technical failure.

66 Hawk Trainers for IAF 
*46. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: W ill the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have approved British-made 
66 Hawk Trainers for IAF; 
(b) if so, the details of the agreement entered into between 
Government and the Royal Air Force; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the British Aero Space is asking for 
US$ 50 million for 'man-hour design work'; 
(d) if so, whether it is also a fact that British Aero Space is of the view 
that if man-hour design work char ges are not paid, the deal would be 
scrapped and it will not stick to committed price and timing; and 
(e) if so, the steps Government are taking or propose to take for 
smooth execution of the agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) 
to (e) Government have approved the induction of 66 Hawk Advanced Jet 
Trainer (AJT) aircraft from M/s. BAe Systems Limited (BAeS), United 
Kingdom, for the Indian Air Force (IAF). 24 of such aircraft would be 
supplied by BAeS in flyaway condition and 42 will be licensed 
manufactured in India by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). 
Contracts and License Agreement have been signed in this regard 
with BAeS, and not with the Royal Air Force (RAF). Till the new aircraft 
are available for the IAF, as an in terim measure, 75 IAF pilots will be 
trained in UK in terms of the Contract. 
The delivery of the 24 aircraft is expected to commence from 
September, 2007 and would be completed by February, 2008. The delivery 
of the 42 aircraft by HAL is expected to commence from March, 2008 and 
would be completed by May, 2010. 
BAeS have neither asked for 50 million US Dollars for "man-hour 
design work", nor have they threatened that the deal would be scrapped or 
that they would not stick to the committed price and timing.

Quality and price of Indian coal vis-a-vis other countries 
†58. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minister of COAL 
AND MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the quality of coal being produced in the 
country is assessed low in comparison to the coal being produced and 
sold by other countries in the international market; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
43 

RAJYA SABHA   [7 July, 2004] 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that besides quality, the comparative 
price of Indian coal is higher as well; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) what are the Government's plans to bring the quality and price of 
Indian coal at par with the international level? 
THE MINISTER FOR COAL AND MINES (SHRI SHIBU SOREN):(a) 
It is a fact that our country is endowed with generally poor quality coal 
compared to many other coal producing countries principally due to the 
nature of coal deposits. 
(b) and (c) The price of Indian coal is based on useful heat value 
(UHV) for non-coking coal and ash percentage for coking coal whereas 
that of imported non-coking coal is based on gross calorific value (GCV) 
and for coking coal, it is based on ash per cent which is much lower than 
Indian coal. The average pit head sale value of Indian coal is one of the 
lowest on per tonne basis in rupee terms when compared to the CIF 
price in the international market. However, the delivered price of Indian 
coal upon transportation over long distance to various consumption points 
including transportation cost is substantially higher and varies depending 
on the distance of transport. The foreign coals being superior in terms of 
ash content and unit heat value, the cost of Indian coal on per therm 
basis is higher in certain coastal locations. 
(d) Indian coal being inherently of inferior quality in nature cannot 
in general be brought at par with International Coal. However by resorting 
to coal beneficiation the ash conten t of Indian coal can be reduced to 
some extent and its heat value can be increased. The Government has 
encouraged setting up of coal benefic iation plants by the BOO (Build 
Own Operate) operators in different coalfields to make available washed 
coal to the needy consumers. 
The average pithead sale value of Indian coal is one of the lowest 
on per tonne basis in rupee terms and compares well to the CIF price in 
the international market.

Co-ordination between various agencies in the power sector 
71. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that there is a need for co-ordination 
between various organizations and agencies like Power Grid Corporation 
and others to ensure that while laying power lines and building transmission 
towers some specific route is followed; 
(b) if so, details of possibilities explored in this regard; 
(c) the details of steps proposed to increase safety and economy in 
such operations; and 
(d) the steps proposed to avoid duplication of work by various 
agencies? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) The 
transmission systems in the country  are executed by Power Grid 
Corporation of India Ltd., State Electricity Boards, etc. in a coordinated 
manner in accordance with the plan prepared by the Central Electricity 
Authority. The transmission systems are evolved after considering various 
aspects like optimum utilization of existing transmission systems and the 
transmission systems being planned/executed by other agencies to avoid 
any duplication. The routes of t he transmission lines are decided in 
accordance with the provisions of Indian Electricity Rules and the Indian 
Standard 5613 (Part 2/Section 1), 1985. 
(c) In order to ensure economy and safety in implementation of the 
transmission lines, among others, the following are kept in view. 
(i) It is advantageous to lay the line near to and along roadway or 
railway. 
(ii) The route should be as short and as straight as possible. 
(iii) Good farming areas, uneven te rrain, religious places, civil and 
defence installations, industries, aerodromes and their approach 
and take off funnels, public and private premises, ponds, tank, 
lakes, gardens and plantations should be avoided as far as 
practicable. 
(iv) Cost of securing and clearing right-of-way, making access roads 
and time required for these works should be minimum. 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [7 July, 2004] 
 (v) Crossing with permanent objects, such as railway lines and roads 
should be minimum and preferably at right angles. 
(vi) Difficult and unsafe approaches should be avoided. 
(vii) The line should be away from the buildings containing explosives, 
bulk storage, oil tanks, oil or gas pipelines. 
(viii) Care is taken to avoid historical monuments, forests and wild 
life sanctuaries, village, habitations, etc. to the extent possible. 
(ix) Clearance from the Electrical Inspector of Central Electricity 
Authority is obtained before commissioning the line.

India as global outsourcing for Textiles 
76. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India is set to emerge as a global 
outsourcing destination for textiles with an export potential of ten billion 
dollars in the next two-three years; 
(b) how are the Indian textile expor ts expected to improve after 
phasing out the quotas by the year end; 
(c) whether McKinsey Report has said that Indian exports grow at 
the rate of 15-18 per cent and would reach 25-30 billion dollars by 2013; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKER SINH VAGHELA): 
(a) and (b) As per W.T.O Agreement on Textiles & Clothing (ATC), the 
discriminatory quota regime governing international trade in textiles and 
clothing would be completely phased out with effect from 1 st January 
2005. The liberalised trading regime would result in increased international 
trade in textiles and clothing thus providing greater export opportunities. 
Government has been taking continuous measures to provide an enabling 
environment for the industry to improve its efficiency and productivity to 
meet the emerging global competition. 
According to several recent studies, India is going to emerge as an 
alternative source of supply to China. India's growth in exports will be 
driven by value added made-ups and apparel as India has comparative 
advantages over its competitors in relation to (i) availability of relatively 
inexpensive and skilled workforce (ii) design expertise (iii) large production 
base of basic raw material like home grown cotton, yarns and fabrics 
and (iv) availability of wide range of textiles. 
(c) and (d) The study by M/s McKinsey & Company has been 
commissioned by DHL and not by the Government. As per study report, 
India has the potential advantage of local textile production, competitive 
labour cost, and strong capabilities in particular categories. The report 
inter-alia has estimated that exports could grow at 15% to 18% per annum, 
significantly faster than its historical growth rate of 6% per annum. With 
this, India should be able to capture 5% share of the world market for 
66 

[7 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
apparel exports by 2008, and yield an export value of $25-30 billion by 
2013.

(a) whether Government has a scheme to encourage youth to work 
and be familiar with National Integration; 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme; 
(c) the Government agencies which implement the scheme; 
(d) whether a component of ths scheme involves taking youths to 
different parts of the country to familiarize them with other areas, languages, 
etc; and 
(e) the details of the scheme and how it is being implemented in 
Andhra Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI SUNIL 
DUTT): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Under the Scheme of Promotion of National 
Integration, the Government provides assistance for holding National 
Integration Camps, Inter-State Youth Exchange Programmes, Symposia 
and Seminars, Multi-cultural activities etc. to promote national integration 
and communal harmony among the youth from different parts of the country 
and from diverse religious and cultural backgrounds. 
(c) These schemes are implemented by State Governments, 
Governmental agencies like National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra 
Sangathan, educational institutions  as well as Non-Governmental 
organisations. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. Inter-State Youth Exchange Programme is a 
programme under the scheme of Promotion of National Integration 
aims at facilitating the visit of youth living and working in one State to other 
States(s) for familiarization with environment, family life, social customs, 
languages, different culture etc. of the people living in different parts of the 
country. 
The Scheme does not provide State-wise allocations. The viable 
proposals received from various States are considered and assistance is 
released. During the last three years, a total amount of Rs. 42.90 lakhs 
has been sanctioned to 25 organisations in Andhra Pradesh.

Upgradation Fund to Rs. 2 crore and set up a research and design centre

community. Hence, I request the Government of India to immediately accept 
these suggestions and save weavers from committing suicide in Andhra 
Pradesh.

Demand for Providing Better Security to Senior 
Citizens 
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ (Jammu & Kashmir): Sir, the lives of senior 
citizens have become vulnerable by the day. In most cases, senior citizens 
who were killed happened to be living alone as their children lived abroad 
for studies or for employment. The murders of senior citizens have been 
occurring in Delhi almost on a regular basis. The killers keep an eye on 
vulnerable citizens and they strike when it is convenient to them. 
The tragic aspect of this "Murder Game" is that instead of police 
keeping watch on the would-be assassins, it is the criminals who keep a 
watch on the police. The assassins strike when they find that police is 
complacent and the senior citizens are helpless. 
In cases of murders of senior citizens at Vasant Kunj and elsewhere 
in Delhi, it was found that the polic e had not even maintained lists of 
senior citizens living in a particular vicinity. This kind of latitude on the part 
of the police is unacceptable to the civil society and, therefore, there is 
public resentment against law enforcing agencies. 
As for Delhi, the House should know very immediately as to how 
many murders occured in a particular period say, one year, closing on 
31.3.2004, what measures were taken to prevent organised killings of 
senior citizens and whether complete lists of senior citizens are available 
with them. 
Thank you, Sir.

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (TAMIL NADU): Mr. Vice Chairman, Sir 
first of all, I submit that the first Railway Budget of this new Government is 
totally disappointing. Sir, it doesn't even have a vision of development of 
Indian Railways in the next five years. Indian Railways, which serves as a 
basic infrastructure for the movement of passenger and freight has to be 
strengthened considerably. But this Budget doesn't reveal any plan for its 
proper development. The investment plan for 2004-05 is totally unimpressive. 
This leads us to believe that most promises will not actually be kept. 
Sir, the main feature in this Budget seems to be announcement 
without any proper funding. Sir, the Budget, according to me, is like an 
election eve Budget by not touching the passenger and freight services. 
I understand the problems of this Government in presenting a 
comprehensive Budget since they have been in office for hardly two 
months. The Railway Minister will do well in curbing dacoity in trains 
passing through Bihar. While the elections to Bihar Assembly round the 
corner, he should concentrate his energies in tackling dacoity in rains 
passing through the State. It looks like the Railway Board and the Railway 
Ministry belong to Bihar. Since Independence, the Railway Ministers of 
the country have come from the Stat e for over 30 years. We had L.N. 
Mishra, Kedar Pandey, Jagjivan Ram, Ram Vilas Paswan, Nitish Kumar 
and now Lalu Prasad. It looks as though the Indian Railways belong to 
Bihar and Bihar is the Indian Railways. For example, a State like Tamil 
Nadu never had a full-fledged Central Cabinet Minsiter handling railways 
ever since independence.

Sir, no wonder the Railway Minister himself has acknowledged in 
this Budget speech that Tamil Nadu is one of the neglected States so far 
as development of Railways is concerned. The railways in Tamil Nadu is 
very backward and has nearly 75 per cent of the tracks in meter gauge. 
The State has the highest concentration of meter gauge in the whole of 
India. The entire railway track from Chennai to Kanyakumari has a single 
track. As far as the railway system is concerned, Tamil Nadu lives in the 
18th Century. From an analysis of the fund allocation for gauge conversion 
projecs shows that the amount allocate d in the current Budget on this 
account is very, very meagre. At this rate of fund flow from Railways, it will 
take another century to complete the ongoing gauge conversion projects 
in Tamil Nadu. 
So, Sir, the casual attitude of the Minister towards the doubling project 
is seen, when he sanctioned hardly Rs. 3 crores for doubling of Madurai to 
Tindukal section which is hardly 2 per  cent of the single railway line 
connecting Madras Egmore to Kanyakumari. This project would take 15 
years to complete at this current rate of fund flow. It will take two centuries 
to complete the entire doubling projects from Chennai to Kanyakumari. 
We now talk in terms of linking Kashmir to Kanyakumari for national 
integration. Is this the way to allocate funds for such crucial project? Even 
the hometown of the President of India, Dr. Abdul Kalam, Rameshwaram, 
has received a raw deal from Lalu Prasad Yadav's Budget. He has hardly 
sanctioned Rs. 25 crores for the project while the total cost of the Madurai 
to Rameshwaram gauge conversion project is Rs. 343 crores. But in this 
Budget, only Rs. 25 crores is sanctioned. Sir, I, therefore, would demand 
a special fund be earmarked for completion of gauge conversion projects 
in Tamil Nadu considering the fact that over 80 per cent of the railway lines 
in the State is meter gauge. 
The Railways are promoting the coach factory at Kapurthala at the 
cost of Integral Coach Factory, Perambur in Tamil Nadu. While 50 years 
old Integral Coach Factory is langui shing for want of funds now. All 
modernisation projects of coach building are being sanctioned for Kapurthala 
factory only. I condemn this step-motherly treatment being given to the 
Integral Coach Factory in Tamil Nadu. 
Another area where the State is lagging behind is the Metropolitan

80 to 90 kms. of track in the last six years, the Metropolitan Railway
